name: 3 platform requirements for agentic engineering
description:
Agentic engineering only works if the platform underneath it can support autonomous action safely. Justin Billig and Dan Rye, co-founders of Tensure, break down the three platform capabilities engineering organizations need to move agents out of experimentation and into production: a controlled action layer, identity and guardrails, and a feedback loop.

**You'll come away knowing:**

1. How to build a controlled action layer that exposes approved capabilities to agents through APIs, Infrastructure as Code, and GitOps rather than direct infrastructure access.
2. How to give each agent an identity, scoped permissions, and explicit boundaries so autonomy stays bounded and humans approve what matters.
3. How to close the feedback loop with observability, testing, policy checks, SLOs, and audit data so agents know whether an action worked and can respond when it didn't.

name: (CS)²AI Online™ REPLAY: Top 20 Secure PLC Coding Practices
description:
Industrial Control Systems (ICS also referred to as OT or Operational Technology, consisting of SCADA, PLC, DCS etc.) have historically been insecure by design. Several years into customizing and applying best practices from IT gave rise to secure protocols, use of encryption, network segmentation & isolation etc. However, to date, there has not been a focus on using the characteristic features in the PLCs and DCS for security, or how to code/program PLCs with security in mind. This project – inspired by existing Secure Coding Practices for IT – fills that gap. The aim of this project is to provide guidelines to engineers that are creating software (ladder logic, functional charts etc.) to help improve the security posture of Industrial Control Systems, by leveraging the natively available functionality in the PLC/DCS/SCADA. Little or no additional software tools or hardware is needed to implement these practices. They can all be fit into the normal PLC programming and operating workflow. More than security expertise, good knowledge of the PLCs to be protected, their logic, and the underlying process, is needed for implementing these practices.

Using these practices always has security benefits – mostly either reducing the attack surface or enabling faster troubleshooting if a security incident were to happen. But many practices have more benefits than “only” security. Some also make PLC code more reliable, easier to debug and maintain, easier to communicate, and potentially also leaner. Also, the secure PLC coding practices not only help users in the event of a malicious attack but also make PLC code more robust to withstand accidental misconfiguration or human error.

Our speaker is Vivek Ponnada, Currently the SVP Growth & Strategy for Frenos. During this webcast was the Director of Regional Sales for Nozomi Networks in Western Canada.

name: Plain Language: A Fireside Chat with Katherine Spivey
description:
Plain language is one of those ideas that sounds simple—until you try to make it work across complex organizations, technical subject matter, policy requirements, competing stakeholders, and real-world constraints.

For this special in-person Content Strategy DC gathering, we’re sitting down with **Katherine Spivey**, one of the DC area’s best-known and longest-standing champions of plain language, for an informal conversation about what it really takes to make information clearer and more useful.

Katherine has spent decades at the intersection of writing, editing, web content, accessibility, communications, and public service. She currently leads GSA’s plain language program and has trained hundreds of federal employees in clearer communication. For more than a decade, she also served as co-chair of the Plain Language Action and Information Network (PLAIN), helping build a community of practitioners across the federal government and supporting PlainLanguage.gov.

Longtime members of the DC content community may also know Katherine from her leadership of DC Web Women, where she served two terms as president, or from her years of teaching, training, speaking, editing, and generally encouraging people to explain things like actual humans.

Rather than a formal presentation, CSDC hosts will guide a fireside-style conversation with Katherine about plain language in practice: what makes it difficult, what makes it work, how the discipline has evolved, and what content professionals should be thinking about now. We’ll also open the conversation to the room, so bring your questions, experiences, frustrations, and favorite examples.

We’re keeping this gathering intentionally small and conversational at **Teaism**, a local tea house serving teas alongside curries, bento boxes, and other Asian-inspired dishes. Come ready for good food, good conversation, and a chance to spend an evening talking shop with someone who has helped shape plain language practice in Washington and well beyond it.

**Please note:** Katherine is participating in this event with the permission of the U.S. General Services Administration (GSA), but she is speaking in her personal capacity and not on behalf of GSA. Her views are her own.

name: Building Privacy Preserving Token Applications Using Panurus
description:
Panurus ([https://github.com/LFDT-Panurus](https://github.com/LFDT-Panurus)) is an open-source framework for building token-based applications that preserve transactional privacy while remaining fully auditable and interoperable across ledgers. In this talk, we'll walk through how Panurus's driver-based architecture lets developers plug in different token technologies — from Fabtoken to zero-knowledge schemes — behind a common transaction lifecycle (Request → Assemble → Sign → Commit), and how this enables privacy-preserving applications without locking you into a single blockchain or cryptographic scheme.

We'll also spotlight two mentorship programs currently pushing Panurus's capabilities forward:

**\- EVM Network Driver** — extending Panurus with support for EVM-compatible chains, bringing privacy-preserving tokens to Ethereum and its ecosystem.
**\- zkat\-snark Driver** — introducing a zk-SNARK-based anonymous token driver, expanding Panurus's toolkit for confidential, provably-correct transactions.

Come see how these efforts are shaping Panurus's roadmap, and how you can get involved.

**Zoom Meeting Link**: [https://zoom.us/my/hyperledger.community.3?pwd=UE90WHhEaHRqOGEyMkV3cldKa2d2dz09](https://zoom.us/my/hyperledger.community.3?pwd=UE90WHhEaHRqOGEyMkV3cldKa2d2dz09)

3\. A working pattern you can adapt to your own IaC tooling, and a realistic view of what agentic remediation can and can't do today, including where human review still belongs.

name: GPU Detective Stories: PyTorch Recompiles & Hidden Bottlenecks
description:
**Monday, November 16, 2026 · 9:00–10:00 AM PST · Online**
**Zoom link:** [https://us02web.zoom.us/j/82308186562](https://us02web.zoom.us/j/82308186562)
Join us for two deep dives into hidden AI performance costs: surprise PyTorch recompilations during inference and compute, memory, and communication bottlenecks in Jev training.
**Talk #0: Introductions and Meetup Updates**
by Chris Fregly and Antje Barth
**Talk #1: The Recompile Ambush: Taming PyTorch Inference Spikes**
by Chaim Rand
`torch.compile` can accelerate steady-state inference, yet a guard failure on a new input shape or layout can trigger an expensive recompilation in the request path. Drawing on his latest post, Chaim will compare six approaches using a dynamic graph-neural-network example: cache preloading, bounded recompilation with eager fallback, Dynamo and input-layout tuning, warmup seeding, background compilation, and ahead-of-time compilation with `torch.export` and AOTInductor. He’ll explain their tradeoffs and how the right choice depends on the model, input distribution, runtime environment, and latency requirements.
**Bio:** Chaim Rand is a machine-learning algorithm developer who writes about PyTorch and practical AI/ML performance optimization.
**Based on:** [Overcoming the PyTorch Recompilation Dilemma in Real-Time Inference Workloads](https://chaimrand.medium.com/overcoming-the-pytorch-recompilation-dilemma-in-real-time-inference-workloads-069fac5485cd)
**Talk #2: Follow the Profile: Hunting Jev’s GPU Bottlenecks**
by Israel Ogbole, Co-founder and CEO of Zymtrace
Israel will explore the latest Zymtrace/TypeSafe case study on training and serving Jev. He’ll discuss how continuous CPU/GPU profiling and MCP-accessible profile data supported an iterative optimization loop across compute, memory, communication, and inference synchronization. The published case study reports approximately 46% higher training throughput on the same hardware after three successive changes, plus approximately 10% better inference performance after removing a hidden device-to-host synchronization. The talk will focus on how the team found each bottleneck, measured each change, and identified the next constraint.
**Bio:** Israel Ogbole is co-founder and CEO of Zymtrace, which develops continuous CPU/GPU profiling tools for performance optimization.
**Based on:** [How TypeSafe achieved 46% higher GPU throughput training Jev — with the help of Zymtrace](https://zymtrace.com/article/typesafe-zymtrace/)

The problem with traditional bridges.
Core trust model.

A powerful GPU can spend plenty of time waiting. What is it waiting for—and how do you find out?
**Talk #0: Welcome and Meetup Updates**
by Chris Fregly and Antje Barth
**Talk #1: From “Why Is This Slow?” to a Faster Kernel**
by Dr. Rajat “Raj” Dandekar, Co-founder of Vizuara
Join Raj for a focused tour of the engineering behind fast AI kernels, drawing on Vizuara’s Kernel Engineering course on Maven. We’ll connect the roofline model to CUDA execution and the GPU memory hierarchy, then look at how profiling guides optimizations such as coalesced memory access, tiling, and tensor-core use. Matrix multiplication and attention provide context for seeing how those ideas fit together in modern AI workloads, including FlashAttention.
The goal is a practical way to decide what to measure, which bottleneck matters, and whether an optimization helped. The session is dedicated to Raj’s talk, with time for audience questions.
**Who it’s for:** Engineers comfortable with Python or basic PyTorch. Prior CUDA or C++ experience is not required.
**Bio:** Dr. Rajat Dandekar is a co-founder of Vizuara and a Kernel Engineering course instructor. He holds a PhD in Mechanical Engineering from Purdue University and BTech and MTech degrees from IIT Madras.
**Based on:** [Kernel Engineering: From CUDA Foundations to Frontier AI Kernels](https://maven.com/rajat-dandekar/kernel-engineering)
